items.title: 67251_Chuck Green oral history interview
items.q: I even heard the famous Irish singer ... I heard Duke Ellington -- he was with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers at the time. So I think I got jazz oriented from listening at those records

ctx.x: Where had you heare these performers?

Well, in Fitzgerald, Georgia, a lady used to play a record. She had a graphinola, and she used to let me play records, you know. I used to run errands for her. She liked White Castle hamburgers, was a nice old lady, she was, and she says that her husband was in import -- export and import, whatever. And he had all these kind of records, and she would let me -- that was kind of like a tip, you know.

But she loved them -- those White Castle hamburgers. At that time I think they was about seven cents a piece, two for 12 cents, something like that, they had. And she was letting me play these records, you see. And I got familiar with these different people, singers, the famous ones, you know, and I heard all of them at that time -- Ethel Waters, as I said, and Morton Downey, and I even heard the famous Irish singer -- what's his name -- and Caruso, Enrico Caruso at the time, you know.

ctx.x: groups that were forming at this particular time?

Oh, yeah. Well, this group that formed before was born into the jazz festival, the full -- the Harlem All-Stars. That was with Illinois Jacquet, Milt Buckner and people like that; the great little jazz, Roy Eldridge. He's being held over now here in the -- in Foreign City at Jimmy Woods (sic) Ryan's, you know. And Jimmy Woods -- by the way, one of Roof Ellington's late brothers finds, he's a bassist. He lives over there in Paris. He was in the virtuso musicians we were with.

items.title: 67251_Chuck Green oral history interview
items.q: Kings would walk back stage or rise up in the audience and say -- ask a question, you know. That's how important he was.

ctx.x: MR. GREEN: Well, there are different dancers, see. There were other dancers on the show with Duke Ellington at that time. It was his tour, see. This is the days of the big band era, you see. Just arriving, but I mean he was a big band before the big band era because he was with McKinney's Cotton Pickers, you see. And he inherited that orchestra, see, which became Duke Ellington and his Orchestra, you see. Especially then, and he was always in great demand because he was -- I think

they would call him the forager of that instrument which is known as piano, you know. He eventually said that the pianist walks in -- comes in and steals the show, see. He had sayings, he was very educational everywhere he was at, you see. He was a gourmet and all this. People had to be very diplomatic, you know, and on their toes at all times, because the most important people in the world used to try to visit Duke Ellington. Kings would walk back stage or rise up in the audience and say -- ask a question, you…
So, how was the show structured?
